Yes, the story has an appropriate balance between scene and summary/exposition. 

The narrative unfolds primarily as a continuous, real-time scene during a morning ferry crossing. It uses vivid sensory details (the fog, the smell of mud, the humming of the cable), character actions, and brief, realistic dialogue to bring the moment to life. Woven seamlessly into this present-time scene are brief, well-placed moments of exposition and summary—such as Ilse's twenty-three years of experience on the river, Wessel's history with his sold dairy cows, the new residents in the old rectory, and the closed bridge in Dannenberg. This background information enriches the characters and setting without halting the momentum of the real-time crossing, creating a well-paced and engaging atmosphere.
